purpose: Atorvastatin is used to lower your bad cholesterol (LDL) and triglycerides, while raising your good cholesterol (HDL). It helps reduce your risk of heart attack, stroke, and other heart problems. Doctors often prescribe it for people with high cholesterol or heart disease risk factors.
how_it_works: Your liver naturally makes cholesterol, and atorvastatin works by blocking a key enzyme in your liver called HMG-CoA reductase that is responsible for producing it. By slowing down cholesterol production, your liver then pulls more bad cholesterol out of your blood to compensate. The result is lower cholesterol levels circulating in your bloodstream, which keeps your arteries healthier.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are muscle aches or soreness, headache, upset stomach, diarrhea, and mild joint pain. Some people also notice mild nausea or fatigue, especially when first starting the medication. Most side effects are mild and often improve over time.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have severe muscle pain, weakness, or dark-colored urine, as this can rarely signal a serious muscle condition called rhabdomyolysis. Avoid drinking large amounts of grapefruit juice, as it can increase the drug's level in your blood and raise side effect risk. Do not take this medication if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as it can harm the baby. Let your doctor know about all other medications you take, since some can interact with atorvastatin.
typical_dosing: Atorvastatin is usually taken once a day, at any time of day, with or without food. The typical starting dose is 10 mg to 20 mg per day, and your doctor may gradually increase it up to 80 mg per day depending on your cholesterol levels and response. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember.
